title: Photosynthesis
text: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food. Using sunlight, the green pigment chlorophyll in the leaves converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose, and oxygen is released as a by-product. The overall equation is 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. Photosynthesis mainly takes place in the chloroplasts of leaf cells, and carbon dioxide enters the leaf through tiny pores called stomata.

title: Respiration
text: Respiration is the process that releases energy from food. In aerobic respiration, glucose is broken down using oxygen into carbon dioxide and water, and a large amount of energy is released, stored as ATP. When oxygen is not available, anaerobic respiration takes place: yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide, while human muscle cells produce lactic acid, which causes cramps after hard exercise.

title: The cell and its organelles
text: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life. The nucleus contains the genetic material and controls the activities of the cell. Mitochondria are called the powerhouse of the cell because they carry out aerobic respiration and produce ATP. Plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose and chloroplasts, which animal cells do not have.

title: DNA and genes
text: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the molecule that carries hereditary information. It has a double helix structure, first described by Watson and Crick in 1953. DNA is made of four bases: adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine. Adenine always pairs with thymine and guanine always pairs with cytosine. A gene is a section of DNA that carries the code for one protein.

title: Mendel and heredity
text: Gregor Mendel, known as the father of genetics, studied inheritance using pea plants. In a monohybrid cross between pure tall and pure dwarf plants, all plants of the F1 generation were tall, showing that tallness is the dominant trait. When F1 plants were self-pollinated, the F2 generation showed tall and dwarf plants in the ratio 3:1.

title: Human digestive system
text: Digestion begins in the mouth, where the enzyme salivary amylase starts breaking down starch. In the stomach, hydrochloric acid kills germs and the enzyme pepsin begins the digestion of proteins. Most digestion and absorption of food happen in the small intestine, whose inner wall has finger-like projections called villi that increase the surface area for absorption. Bile from the liver helps in the digestion of fats by breaking them into small droplets.

title: Nervous system
text: The nervous system controls and coordinates the activities of the body. The basic unit of the nervous system is the neuron, or nerve cell. The junction between two neurons is called a synapse. A reflex action is a quick, automatic response to a stimulus, such as pulling the hand away from a hot object; the path it follows is called a reflex arc and it is controlled by the spinal cord.

title: Hormones
text: Hormones are chemical messengers released by endocrine glands directly into the blood. Insulin, made by the pancreas, controls the level of sugar in the blood, and a lack of insulin causes diabetes. The thyroid gland makes thyroxine, which needs iodine; a lack of iodine can cause goitre. Adrenaline, from the adrenal glands, prepares the body for emergencies.

title: Food chains and ecosystems
text: An ecosystem includes all living organisms in an area together with their physical environment. In a food chain, energy flows from producers such as green plants to herbivores and then to carnivores. Only about 10 percent of the energy at one level passes to the next level; this is called the 10 percent law. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.

title: The ozone layer
text: The ozone layer is found in the stratosphere and absorbs most of the harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun. Ozone is a molecule made of three oxygen atoms (O3). Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), once used in refrigerators and aerosol sprays, damage the ozone layer. The Montreal Protocol of 1987 was an international agreement to phase out CFCs.

title: Newton's first law
text: Newton's first law of motion states that an object stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed, unless an unbalanced external force acts on it. This tendency of objects to resist a change in their state of motion is called inertia. The greater the mass of an object, the greater its inertia; this is why passengers fall forward when a moving bus suddenly stops.

title: Newton's second law
text: Newton's second law of motion states that the rate of change of momentum of an object is proportional to the applied force. For a constant mass, this gives the formula F = m x a, where F is force, m is mass and a is acceleration. The SI unit of force is the newton (N); one newton is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s^2.

title: Newton's third law
text: Newton's third law of motion states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. The two forces act on two different objects, so they do not cancel each other. Examples include the recoil of a gun when a bullet is fired and a rocket moving upward by pushing hot gases downward.

title: Gravitation
text: Newton's universal law of gravitation states that every object attracts every other object with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The value of the universal gravitational constant G is 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2. The acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the Earth, g, is about 9.8 m/s^2.

title: Work, energy and power
text: Work is done when a force moves an object in the direction of the force, and it is calculated as W = F x s. Kinetic energy is the energy of a moving object, given by KE = (1/2) m v^2, and potential energy due to height is PE = m g h. Power is the rate of doing work, and its SI unit is the watt (W), equal to one joule per second. The law of conservation of energy says energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only changed from one form to another.

title: Ohm's law and resistance
text: Ohm's law states that the current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, at constant temperature. It is written as V = I x R, where R is the resistance measured in ohms. The resistance of a wire increases with its length and decreases as its area of cross-section increases. When resistors are connected in series, the total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances.

title: Electric power and energy
text: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is used, given by P = V x I. The SI unit of power is the watt. The commercial unit of electrical energy is the kilowatt-hour (kWh), commonly called one unit of electricity; 1 kWh equals 3.6 x 10^6 joules. Electric fuses protect circuits by melting and breaking the circuit when too much current flows.

title: Magnetic effects of current
text: A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it, as first observed by Hans Christian Oersted. Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field and is the principle behind the electric motor. Electromagnetic induction, discovered by Michael Faraday, is the production of current by a changing magnetic field, and it is the principle of the electric generator.

title: Reflection of light
text: Reflection is the bouncing back of light from a surface. According to the laws of reflection, the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane. A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image of the same size as the object. Concave mirrors are used in torches and shaving mirrors, while convex mirrors are used as rear-view mirrors in vehicles because they give a wider field of view.

title: Refraction of light
text: Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one medium into another, because light travels at different speeds in different media. The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in that medium. Snell's law states that sin i / sin r is constant for a given pair of media. A pencil placed in water appears bent because of refraction.

title: The human eye and its defects
text: The human eye focuses light on the retina using a convex eye lens whose focal length is adjusted by the ciliary muscles; this ability is called the power of accommodation. In myopia, or near-sightedness, a person cannot see distant objects clearly, and it is corrected using a concave lens. In hypermetropia, or far-sightedness, nearby objects are not clear, and it is corrected using a convex lens.

title: Sound
text: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium to travel, so it cannot travel through vacuum. Sound waves in air are longitudinal waves made of compressions and rarefactions. The speed of sound in air is about 343 m/s at 20 degrees Celsius, and sound travels faster in solids than in gases. Humans can hear frequencies from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; sound above 20,000 Hz is called ultrasound.

title: Acids, bases and pH
text: Acids taste sour and turn blue litmus red, while bases taste bitter and turn red litmus blue. The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a solution is, from 0 to 14. A pH of 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic. When an acid reacts with a base, salt and water are formed; this reaction is called neutralisation. Toothpaste is basic and is used to neutralise acids in the mouth that cause tooth decay.

title: Types of chemical reactions
text: In a combination reaction, two or more substances combine to form one product, such as calcium oxide reacting with water to form slaked lime. In a decomposition reaction, one substance breaks down into simpler substances. In a displacement reaction, a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one from its compound, as when iron displaces copper from copper sulphate solution. Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen, and reduction is the opposite; reactions where both happen are called redox reactions.

title: The periodic table
text: The modern periodic table, based on the work of Henry Moseley, arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number. It has 18 vertical columns called groups and 7 horizontal rows called periods. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons and similar chemical properties. Dmitri Mendeleev had earlier arranged elements by atomic mass and left gaps for elements not yet discovered.

title: Carbon and its compounds
text: Carbon forms a very large number of compounds because of catenation, its ability to form long chains with other carbon atoms, and because it has a valency of four. Carbon forms covalent bonds by sharing electrons. Hydrocarbons with only single bonds are called alkanes, those with a double bond are alkenes and those with a triple bond are alkynes. Diamond and graphite are two allotropes of carbon; graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.

title: Metals and non-metals
text: Metals are usually lustrous, malleable, ductile and good conductors of heat and electricity. Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Non-metals are usually brittle and poor conductors, but graphite is an exception that conducts electricity. Rusting of iron happens when iron reacts with oxygen and moisture, and it can be prevented by painting, oiling or galvanisation, which means coating iron with zinc.

title: The water cycle
text: The water cycle is the continuous movement of water on the Earth. Water from oceans, rivers and lakes evaporates due to the heat of the Sun, and plants release water vapour through transpiration. The vapour cools and condenses to form clouds, and the water returns to the Earth as precipitation in the form of rain, snow or hail. The water then flows back to water bodies or seeps into the ground as groundwater.

title: Sources of energy
text: Renewable sources of energy, such as solar, wind, hydro and biomass, can be replaced naturally and will not run out. Non-renewable sources, such as coal, petroleum and natural gas, are fossil fuels formed over millions of years and will run out. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming. Solar cells convert sunlight directly into electricity and are usually made of silicon.

title: Evolution
text: Evolution is the gradual change in the characteristics of a species over many generations. Charles Darwin proposed the theory of natural selection, which states that organisms with useful variations survive and reproduce more, so those variations become common over time. Homologous organs, such as the forelimbs of humans, bats and whales, have the same basic structure but different functions, and they show common ancestry. Fossils provide evidence of how organisms have changed over time.
